title: Where Jesus appears, salvation appears
english: Wherever Jesus appears, there salvation is also. If he sees a tax collector sitting at the tax booth, he makes him an apostle and evangelist. If he is buried among the dead, he raises the dead. He grants sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf. He goes around the pools, not looking at the buildings but healing the sick.

For in Jerusalem there was a sheep pool with five porticoes: four running around it, and the fifth in the middle, where a crowd of the sick lay. And there was great unbelief among the Jews. But the physician and healer of souls and bodies granted healing in due measure, healing first the one who had suffered the longest, so that he might be released more quickly from his pains. For it was not one day that he lay there, nor a second, nor a first month or a year, but thirty-eight years. Lying there with his long illness, he was known to those who saw him, and he showed the working of the one who heals. For the paralytic was recognized by everyone because of the length of time. The great physician showed his power, but he was rejected by those who received him badly.

Going around the pool, he saw him. He did not learn from questioning, but from divine working he supplied what was lacking. Seeing, not asking, how long he had lain there, he saw and knew, the one who knew even before he saw. For if in matters of the heart he had no need for anyone to ask him about a person, for he himself knew what was in the person (John 2:25), how much more did he know about illnesses, whose onset comes from outside?

He saw a certain man lying there, weighed down by a very great illness. For he had a heavy burden of sins and the long-lasting pain of disease. To this man he speaks a question that was longed for: "Do you want to become well?" (John 5:6) He did not say anything else, but left it in the middle ground of the question. For the question was double. Since not only his body was sick but also his soul, according to what was said by him later: "See, you have become well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you" (John 5:14), he asked him: "Do you want to become well?" O the power of the great physician, who places help upon the willing! For since salvation comes from faith, he heard the "Do you want," so that the willing might bring about the working. This saying belongs to Jesus alone. It does not belong to physical physicians. For those who heal physical diseases cannot say to everyone: "Do you want to become well?" But Jesus grants even the willing, receives the believing, and gives the gift without payment.

Once the Savior was passing along the road, and two blind men were sitting there, blind in body but enlightened in mind. For the one whom the scribes did not know, the blind men pointed out by crying aloud. The Pharisees had learned the law and studied it from childhood to old age, and they had grown old in ignorance, saying: "We do not know where this man is from." For he came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1:11). But the blind men cried out, saying: "Son of David, have mercy on us." And the one whom those who had learned the law did not know, those who had eyes that did not serve them for reading knew. The Savior came to them and said: "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" And: "What do you want me to do for you?" (Matthew 20:32) He did not say, "What do you want me to say to you," but, "What do you want me to do for you." For he was a maker and life-giver, not now beginning to make. For his Father is always working (John 5:17), and he works together with the Father, and he was the maker of all things by the nod of the Father. He alone, begotten from the Father alone without mediation, asks the blind men, saying: "What do you want me to do for you?"

orientation: Cyril opens his homily by declaring that wherever Jesus appears there is salvation, and he begins describing the pool of Bethesda and the paralytic who lay there thirty-eight years.
